Hi Alex —

Thanks for the clear asks. I put together a short proposal attached (slo-proposal-v3.pdf) and a sample CSV with measurement examples. Key points up front:

- Measurement windows: we compute p50 and p95 on a per-route, rolling 30-minute aggregation window by default for latency commitments in the contract. For monthly uptime/latency reporting we publish daily buckets computed from non-overlapping 1-hour windows that roll up to the month.

- Proxy/CDN adjustments: we exclude transit time from documented edge proxies only when a validated edge header is present (x-rw-edge-latency). If no validated header is available, all observed latency is counted in the request's total. For customers routing through a 3rd-party proxy, we offer a "proxy-adjusted" measurement profile during onboarding — this requires a 7-day telemetry baseline.

- Rollforward / grace: when enabling a new route we apply a 72-hour onboarding grace period where we collect telemetry but do not count violations for contractual claims. After that, a 7-day rollforward window is used for initial baseline normalization where we still show raw metrics but do not trigger penalties. Both windows are opt-in in the SOW; standard for hosted customers is 72-hour grace + 7-day rollforward.

- Exceptions: common exception requests include long-tailed customer prompts (documented prompt groups), large model warmups after model switches, and cross-region failovers. We enumerate these in the proposal along with mitigation controls (canary capacity, auto-fallback to compatible models).

Marissa and Karthik are looped for operational and legal alignment. If this looks good to you, we can add the short appendix to the SOW and mark the billing implications section as negotiated.

Best,
Rishi

Technical note from infra: please consider the following operational constraints we highlighted in the attachment.

1) Aggregation semantics: our runtime tags requests with service-hops and kernel-time. For proxy-adjusted profiles we subtract validated edge-hop time from the client-observed time. This is deterministic when the x-rw-edge-latency header is signed by the edge (HMAC) — unsigned headers are ignored to prevent spoofing.

2) Sampling: for very high-throughput routes (>20k rps sustained) we use deterministic reservoir sampling for 1/10 of requests to reduce telemetry costs; the sampling factor is applied uniformly and we scale percentiles appropriately. This is called out in the appendix.

3) Measurement examples: see measurement-samples.csv — note the warmup spike when we change quantization profiles; that spike is a common reason for an exception in the first 24–72 hours.

If FinOps needs the edge header instrumentation but cannot modify their edge, we can also add an ingress probe as an alternative (adds ~50ms overhead max).

-Karthik
SRE Lead, Redwood Inference
